corrected_answer:
Analytical stance under test: batch-composition-and-arrival-process-first - quantization changes how many requests coexist in a batch, and the batch is what actually sets latency.

Hypothesis H41: at fixed offered load and fixed max-num-seqs, the WOQ arm and the BF16 arm differ in mean running-batch-size by less than 5 percent; if they differ by more, any observed TPOT delta is a batching artefact and not a kernel-speed result.

Mechanism. Weight-only quantization (WOQ) reduces the bytes read per weight tile during the GEMM. In the decode phase a transformer step is dominated by weight streaming when the running batch is small: arithmetic intensity is roughly batch_size x tokens_per_step FLOPs per weight byte, so at batch 1 the step is bandwidth-bound and shrinking W from 16 bits to 4 bits can approach a 4x reduction in weight traffic. As the running batch grows, the same weight bytes are amortized over more rows and the GEMM crosses toward compute-bound, at which point the dequantization ALU work is added on top of an operation that was no longer bandwidth-limited. The consequence is that the WOQ speedup is a decreasing function of running batch size, and running batch size is itself an outcome of the scheduler, not an input you set. Freeing HBM by shrinking weights lets the engine admit more concurrent sequences, which raises the batch, which erodes the very speedup you are trying to measure. The two effects move in opposite directions and a single blended throughput number cannot separate them.

Boundary conditions. This decomposition holds for dense decode-heavy serving on a single node. It does not hold when (a) prefill dominates the token mix, because prefill is already compute-bound and WOQ helps little or hurts; (b) an MoE model routes only a fraction of experts per token, changing the effective weight footprint per step; (c) the engine uses chunked prefill and mixes prefill and decode in the same step, which makes "batch size" ambiguous unless you log prefill and decode token counts separately.

Controlled experiment. Fix model weights, tokenizer, engine version, GPU model and clocks, and replay one frozen trace with recorded arrival timestamps (open-loop), not a closed-loop client that self-throttles. Run three arms: BF16 baseline; WOQ with max-num-seqs and gpu-memory-utilization pinned to the BF16 values so the extra HBM is deliberately wasted; WOQ unclamped, allowed to use the freed memory. Arm 2 minus arm 1 isolates the kernel effect. Arm 3 minus arm 2 isolates the capacity effect. Sweep offered load across at least five points spanning 30 to 90 percent of the baseline saturation point, three repeats per point with different RNG seeds, discard the first 120 s as warm-up.

Measurements. Per step: running batch size, waiting queue depth, prefill tokens, decode tokens. Per request: TTFT, TPOT, end-to-end latency, all reported as p50/p95/p99 with bootstrap 95 percent CIs. System: achieved output tokens/s, GPU utilization, HBM occupancy split into weights, KV, activations, fragmentation.

Confounders. Closed-loop clients that hide queueing; unequal KV block counts between arms; CUDA graph capture differing across arms; power or thermal cap differences; a warm page cache for one arm only; different sampling parameters changing sequence length distribution.

Numbers. Any speedup figure I quote here would be an ESTIMATE from the roofline argument above (weight bytes ratio 16/4 = 4x upper bound at batch 1, decaying toward 1x or below as batch grows); nothing is MEASURED on your hardware. The experiment exists to replace those estimates with measurements.

Evidence required and rollback. Ship only if arm-2 TPOT improvement is significant at p95 and the pre-registered quality suite shows no per-slice regression beyond the indifference threshold. Roll back on one config flip if p99 TTFT regresses more than 10 percent, if any quality slice regresses beyond threshold, or if the batch-size logs show the arms were never comparable.

corrected_answer:
Analytical stance under test: numerical-reproducibility-first - the quantized checkpoint must be bit-reproducible from a recorded recipe or no comparison is auditable.

Hypothesis H42: re-running the quantization pipeline twice from the same recipe hash produces byte-identical weight files; if it does not, every downstream quality delta is confounded by an uncontrolled quantization nondeterminism term whose magnitude is unknown.

Mechanism. A WOQ checkpoint is a build artifact produced by a program: a calibration sample, a scale-search or GPTQ/AWQ solver, a group size, a symmetric-or-asymmetric choice, a dtype for scales and zero-points, and a packing layout. Several of these steps use RNG (calibration sampling, sometimes Hessian damping order) and reduction orders that are nondeterministic on GPU. If the pipeline is not seeded and pinned, two "identical" checkpoints differ, and the quality gap between them is a noise floor that must be measured before any BF16-versus-WOQ gap can be called real. Measuring that floor is the cheapest experiment in the whole program and is almost always skipped.

Boundary conditions. Bit-reproducibility is achievable for the quantization step on fixed hardware with fixed library versions and deterministic kernels enabled; it is generally not achievable across GPU architectures or across major library versions. Therefore the reproducibility claim is scoped to one (driver, CUDA, framework, GPU SKU) tuple and must be re-established when any element changes. Inference-time determinism is a separate and weaker guarantee: batching changes reduction order, so identical prompts can yield different logits at different batch sizes even with a fixed checkpoint.

Controlled experiment. Step 1, produce checkpoint A from recipe R with seed s. Step 2, produce checkpoint A' from the same R and s on the same machine; assert sha256(A) == sha256(A'). Step 3, produce checkpoints B1..B5 from R with seeds s1..s5, differing only in calibration sampling. Evaluate all of them on the frozen quality suite at batch size 1 with greedy decoding. The spread across B1..B5 is the quantization noise floor. Step 4, only now compare BF16 against the mean of B1..B5, and require the BF16-versus-WOQ difference to exceed that floor by a pre-registered margin.

Measurements. sha256 of every weight shard; per-tensor max and mean absolute error between dequantized W and original W; per-slice quality scores for each seed with CIs; the standard deviation across seeds as the explicit noise floor.

Confounders. Nondeterministic library kernels, unpinned tokenizer or dataset versions, hidden dependence on file iteration order, mixed CPU/GPU calibration paths, and an evaluation harness that itself has RNG.

Numbers. The claim "5 seeds is enough" is an ESTIMATE: with 5 samples the CI on a standard deviation is wide, so treat it as a lower bound on the floor and prefer 8 to 10 seeds if GPU time allows. No MEASURED value is asserted.

Evidence required and rollback. Publish the recipe file, all shard hashes, the per-seed scores, and the noise floor alongside any headline number. If reproducibility fails, the comparison is not shippable at any effect size; halt and fix the pipeline before spending more GPU hours.

corrected_answer:
Analytical stance under test: prefill-versus-decode-token-mix-first - the token mix decides the sign of the result, so measure the mix before measuring the speedup.

Hypothesis H43: for the production trace, the fraction of GPU time spent in prefill exceeds 40 percent; if so, weight-only quantization cannot deliver the headline decode speedup at the system level and may be net negative.

Mechanism. Prefill processes many tokens per weight load and is compute-bound; decode processes one token per sequence per step and is bandwidth-bound. WOQ shrinks weight bytes, which is a bandwidth remedy. Applying a bandwidth remedy to a compute-bound phase yields no benefit and adds dequantization ALU work, so prefill can slow down. The system-level effect is therefore an Amdahl composition: overall gain is bounded by the decode fraction of GPU time. A workload of 4k-token prompts and 50-token answers is prefill-dominated; a chat workload of 200-token prompts and 500-token answers is decode-dominated. The same checkpoint can look excellent on one and useless on the other, which is why vendor numbers and your numbers disagree without either being dishonest.

Boundary conditions. Applies to standard dense transformers with a KV cache. Prefix caching changes the mix by removing repeated prefill; speculative decoding changes it by making decode steps process multiple tokens and therefore more compute-bound; disaggregated prefill/decode deployments let you apply WOQ only to decode workers, which is the intervention this hypothesis argues for.

Controlled experiment. Phase 0, instrument production for one week and record per-request prompt length, output length, and the engine's own prefill and decode token counters; compute the GPU-time split, not the token-count split, because they differ. Phase 1, replay the recorded trace against BF16 and WOQ arms on identical hardware. Phase 2, if the mix is prefill-heavy, add a fourth arm: disaggregated serving with BF16 prefill workers and WOQ decode workers, and compare cost per served request against the monolithic arms.

Measurements. Prefill and decode GPU-milliseconds per request; the ratio as a distribution not a mean; TTFT (prefill-sensitive) and TPOT (decode-sensitive) reported separately with p50/p95/p99 and CIs; tokens/s per GPU; cost per million output tokens.

Confounders. Chunked prefill blurring the phase boundary; prefix cache hit rate differing between arms or between the trace window and the replay; padding policy inflating prefill tokens; a benchmark harness that uses fixed-length synthetic prompts and therefore fixes the answer in advance.

Numbers. The 40 percent threshold is an ESTIMATE chosen so that even a perfect decode speedup leaves less than a 1.7x whole-system gain by Amdahl arithmetic (1 / (0.4 + 0.6/inf) = 2.5x absolute ceiling, discounted for realistic decode gains); it is a decision threshold, not a measurement.

Evidence required and rollback. Do not approve a WOQ rollout on decode-microbenchmark evidence alone. Require the trace-replay result and the GPU-time split. Roll back if production TTFT p95 regresses beyond 10 percent after deploy, and keep the BF16 checkpoint loadable by a single config flip for the full bake period.

corrected_answer:
Analytical stance under test: safety-and-refusal-behaviour-first - quantization can move alignment behaviour without moving aggregate benchmark scores.

Hypothesis H44: the WOQ arm's refusal rate and jailbreak-resistance rate on a frozen red-team suite are statistically indistinguishable from BF16 at a pre-registered equivalence margin; a benchmark-parity result does not establish this and must not be used as a substitute.

Mechanism. Aggregate accuracy suites average over thousands of items and are insensitive to a behaviour that occupies a small region of input space. Alignment behaviour is exactly such a region: it is concentrated on a minority of prompts and is often carried by low-probability-margin decisions where a small logit perturbation flips the output. WOQ perturbs every weight by a bounded quantization error; per-channel outliers are the largest contributors, and refusal behaviour empirically lives in a fragile part of the decision surface. So a checkpoint can score identically on MMLU-style suites and still refuse less, or over-refuse more, on safety prompts. Averaging hides this by construction, which is a measurement design flaw rather than a surprise.

Boundary conditions. This concerns behavioural drift, not capability loss, and applies whenever the model is user-facing or tool-calling. For a purely internal batch-scoring model with no free-text user input, the risk is lower and the suite can be smaller. Tool-calling models need an additional slice: whether quantization changes the rate of malformed or unauthorized tool calls, since that is a direct operational safety exposure, not just a quality question.

Controlled experiment. Freeze a red-team and over-refusal suite before running any arm, with items stratified into categories and a fixed grading rubric plus a fixed grader (human-audited sample of at least 100 items to establish grader agreement). Run BF16 and WOQ at identical decoding parameters, greedy and temperature-matched sampling as two sub-arms. Use an equivalence test (TOST) against a pre-registered margin rather than a null-hypothesis test, because "we failed to find a difference" is not evidence of equivalence at small n.

Measurements. Per-category refusal rate, jailbreak success rate, over-refusal rate on benign look-alike prompts, malformed tool-call rate, and schema-violation rate, each with binomial CIs; a paired per-item disagreement matrix between arms to find which items flipped.

Confounders. A grader that is itself a model and drifts; sampling temperature differences; system prompt differences; test-set contamination through prior tuning; too few items per category to detect a 2-point change.

Numbers. Sample-size guidance: detecting a 5-percentage-point change in a rate near 10 percent at 80 percent power needs roughly 600 items per arm per category (ESTIMATE from a two-proportion normal approximation); if you have 50 items per category, the study cannot detect anything actionable and should be resized before it is run.

Evidence required and rollback. Require the equivalence result, the per-item flip list, and grader-agreement statistics before rollout. Roll back immediately on any confirmed increase in jailbreak success or unauthorized tool-call rate, regardless of throughput gains; this is a one-way door and should be governed by the safety owner, not the performance owner.

corrected_answer:
Analytical stance under test: shared-cluster-interference-first - an isolated benchmark measures a machine you do not run in production.

Hypothesis H45: the WOQ-versus-BF16 gap measured on a drained node is larger than the gap measured on a co-tenanted node by more than 20 percent relative; if so, the isolated benchmark systematically overstates the production benefit and must not be the basis for the capacity plan.

Mechanism. In production, GPUs share PCIe/NVLink, host memory bandwidth, network, and often the same node with other pods. WOQ's benefit is a reduction in HBM traffic, which is a resource that is local to the GPU; but the end-to-end request path also crosses tokenizer CPU work, host-to-device transfers, network ingress, and possibly a KV transfer for disaggregated or prefix-cache-sharing setups. When those shared paths are congested, they become the binding constraint and the local HBM improvement stops converting into user-visible latency. A drained-node benchmark removes exactly the congestion that would have masked the gain, so it is biased upward by construction. The bias is not noise; it is a systematic direction, which makes it a validity problem rather than a precision problem.

Boundary conditions. The effect is small for single-tenant dedicated inference fleets with generous network headroom. It is large for multi-tenant clusters, for deployments with cross-node KV transfer (RDMA/RoCE paths, GPUDirect RDMA), and for setups where NCCL collectives from a co-located training job compete for the same NICs or NVLink. If tensor parallelism is in use, the all-reduce per layer puts the interconnect on the critical path of every decode step, and WOQ does not shrink activation traffic at all, only weights, so the collective term is unchanged and its relative share grows.

Controlled experiment. Run a 2x2: {BF16, WOQ} x {drained node, node with a pre-registered synthetic co-tenant load}. The co-tenant must be reproducible: a fixed background job with recorded NIC and PCIe utilization, not "whatever was running". Add a third environment level, real production shadow traffic, if a shadow path exists. Randomize arm-to-node assignment and interleave arms in time to defeat drift.

Measurements. Per-arm TTFT/TPOT p50/p95/p99 with CIs; NIC tx/rx bytes and pause frames if RoCE is in play; PCIe and NVLink counters; NCCL collective time per step if TP>1; host CPU steal time; and the drained-versus-loaded gap ratio, which is the actual estimand.

Confounders. Node hardware heterogeneity (different HBM bins, different NIC firmware), NUMA placement differences, MIG or MPS configuration differences, thermal throttling on the loaded node, and unrecorded neighbour churn.

Numbers. The 20 percent threshold is an ESTIMATE serving as a decision rule for "the isolated benchmark is unsafe to extrapolate from". All interconnect utilization figures must be reported as MEASURED counters with the collection method named.

Evidence required and rollback. Capacity plans must cite the loaded-environment number, not the drained one. Roll back or halt expansion if realized production p99 diverges from the loaded-benchmark prediction by more than the pre-registered tolerance, and record the divergence as a model-of-the-system error to be fixed before the next study.

corrected_answer:
Analytical stance under test: cold-start-and-elasticity-first - if the fleet autoscales, load time and replica count are part of the cost function.

Hypothesis H46: the WOQ arm's cold-start time to first healthy request is at least 30 percent lower than BF16; if it is not, the smaller checkpoint is not buying the elasticity benefit it is often credited with, and the cost case must rest on steady-state throughput alone.

Mechanism. A 4-bit checkpoint is roughly a quarter the bytes of BF16 on disk and in HBM, so the naive expectation is proportionally faster loading. In practice the load path includes object-store or network read, page cache behaviour, deserialization, possible on-the-fly repacking of the quantized layout, CUDA context creation, kernel autotuning or CUDA graph capture, and warm-up of the engine's memory pools. Several of those terms are constant with respect to checkpoint size, and repacking can be strictly worse for the quantized artifact. So the size ratio is an upper bound on the load-time ratio and often a loose one. Cold start matters because it sets how aggressively you can scale in during troughs; if scale-in is slow to reverse, you keep replicas warm and never realize the paper savings.

Boundary conditions. Relevant only for elastic or spot-backed fleets, or where failure recovery time is an SLO. Irrelevant for a fixed-size always-on fleet, where the memory saving matters only through replica density. Also note that if WOQ raises per-replica capacity, the fleet needs fewer replicas, which independently reduces the frequency of cold starts; that is a separate and legitimate benefit that this experiment should not conflate with load speed.

Controlled experiment. Measure cold start with the page cache dropped between runs and with it warm, as two sub-conditions, because the difference between them is often larger than the difference between arms. Decompose the timeline with explicit spans: fetch, deserialize, H2D copy, engine init, graph capture, first-token warm-up, health-check pass. Ten repeats per cell. Separately, run a scale-out drill: inject a step increase in load and record time-to-SLO-recovery for each arm.

Measurements. Per-span milliseconds with p50/p95; total time-to-healthy; bytes fetched; peak host RAM during load; number of replicas required to hold the SLO at the trace's peak; realized replica-hours per day under the autoscaler policy.

Confounders. Object-store throttling and cache warmth, image pull time counted or not counted, autoscaler cooldown settings differing between arms, and a health check that passes before the engine is actually warm.

Numbers. The 30 percent threshold is an ESTIMATE derived by discounting the 4x byte ratio for constant-cost spans; the actual span decomposition is what makes it falsifiable. Any claimed replica-hour savings must be reported as MEASURED under a stated autoscaler policy, since the policy, not the checkpoint, dominates that figure.

Evidence required and rollback. Require the span breakdown and the scale-out drill result before crediting elasticity savings in the business case. Roll back the autoscaler policy change, separately from the checkpoint change, if time-to-SLO-recovery regresses; keeping the two changes independently revertible is the point.

Analytical stance under test: adversarial-review-and-blinding-first - the person who wants the result should not be the person who measures it.

Hypothesis H47: an independent analyst, given only anonymized arm labels and the raw measurement artifacts, reaches the same accept/reject decision as the original team; if the decisions diverge, the original conclusion is analyst-dependent and cannot be treated as a fleet-wide fact.

Mechanism. Quantization studies have an unusually large researcher-degrees-of-freedom surface: which quality suite, which slices, which percentile, which warm-up window, which outlier requests to drop, whether to clamp KV capacity, whether to retune the baseline. Each choice is defensible in isolation, and the joint space is large enough that a motivated analyst can reach almost any conclusion without doing anything they would call dishonest. Blinding and pre-registration remove the mechanism, not the intent: if the analysis plan is written and hashed before the data exists, and if the arm labels are hidden during analysis, the degrees of freedom cannot be spent selectively.

Boundary conditions. Full blinding is impossible for measurements that reveal the arm (HBM occupancy makes the 4-bit arm obvious). So blind what can be blinded, the quality grading and the latency analysis, and pre-register what cannot. This is a process control, not a statistical one; it does not substitute for adequate sample size or a correct experimental design.

Controlled experiment. Write the analysis plan first: primary metric, decision rule with thresholds, secondary metrics, exclusion rules, stopping rule, and the exact statistical test. Hash it and commit the hash. Collect data with arms labelled as X and Y by a script that records the mapping to a sealed file. Have a second engineer run the pre-registered analysis and record a decision. Unseal. Compare decisions. Record any deviation from the plan as a labelled deviation with a reason, and report deviations alongside results.

Measurements. The pre-registered primary metric and decision; the independent analyst's decision; a count and list of protocol deviations; and, as a diagnostic, the range of conclusions reachable by plausible alternative analysis choices (a small multiverse or specification-curve analysis).

Confounders. Leakage of arm identity through file names, timestamps, or HBM metrics; an analyst who consulted the team before deciding; post-hoc slice selection presented as pre-registered; and stopping data collection when the result looked good.

Numbers. No MEASURED performance number is asserted by this stance; the single quantity it introduces, the fraction of defensible specifications that reach "ship", is an ESTIMATE until the multiverse analysis is actually run. Where the multiverse analysis is run, report the fraction of specifications that reach "ship" as a MEASURED property of your own analysis flexibility; a headline result that is reached by only a minority of defensible specifications should not be shipped.

Evidence required and rollback. Require the pre-registration hash, the sealed mapping, and both decisions in the review packet. If the independent decision disagrees, do not ship; re-run with a design that removes the ambiguity. Rollback of the deployment remains a single config flip regardless of how confident the analysis was.

corrected_answer:
Analytical stance under test: checkpoint-and-serving-format-coupling-first - the quantized artifact binds you to an engine version, and that coupling is part of the cost.

Hypothesis H48: the WOQ checkpoint loads and produces numerically equivalent outputs on at least two independent serving stacks and across one major version upgrade of the primary stack; if not, the artifact is a single-vendor lock-in with an unpriced migration cost.

Mechanism. A BF16 checkpoint is a nearly universal artifact: any stack can read the tensors. A quantized checkpoint additionally encodes a packing layout, a group size, a scale/zero-point dtype and placement, and sometimes fused-kernel expectations. These are conventions, not standards, and they differ across quantization schemes and across engine versions. The practical consequence is that upgrading the engine, or moving to a different stack for a capacity or cost reason, may require re-quantizing, which means re-running calibration, re-validating quality, and re-doing the safety suite. That recurring cost belongs in the comparison, and it is usually omitted because the first quantization run is treated as a one-time expense.

Boundary conditions. The lock-in is weak when the scheme is widely implemented and the layout is documented; it is strong for bespoke or research-grade schemes and for anything relying on a custom fused kernel. It is also stronger for larger models where re-quantization is expensive in GPU-hours, and for regulated environments where every re-quantization triggers a full revalidation cycle.

Controlled experiment. Take the produced checkpoint and attempt: (a) load on serving stack A at pinned version; (b) load on serving stack B; (c) load on stack A at the next major version; (d) load after a GPU-architecture change if the fleet is heterogeneous. For each that loads, run a fixed prompt set at greedy decoding and compare token-level outputs against the reference; record exact-match rate and the first divergence position. For each that fails, record the failure mode and estimate the re-quantization cost in GPU-hours and engineer-days.

Measurements. Load success matrix; greedy exact-match rate per stack; per-slice quality on each stack that loads; re-quantization GPU-hours (MEASURED from the actual pipeline run) and calendar time for full revalidation.

Confounders. Kernel selection differences producing benign numerical divergence mistaken for a load bug; different default sampling parameters; tokenizer version skew; and comparing against a reference that was itself produced on a different stack.

Do not quote a lock-in cost as a percentage without the underlying GPU-hour and engineer-day figures; those must be MEASURED from the first pipeline run and then multiplied by an ESTIMATED re-quantization frequency (for example, once per major engine upgrade, which for many stacks is several times a year). State the assumed frequency explicitly so a reviewer can challenge it.

corrected_answer:
Analytical stance under test: grouping-granularity-and-outlier-channels-first - the group size is the actual dial, and the fair comparison sweeps it rather than fixing it arbitrarily.

Hypothesis H49: per-slice quality is monotonically non-decreasing as group size shrinks from per-tensor toward 64, and the marginal quality gain from 128 to 64 is smaller than the pre-registered indifference threshold; if quality is non-monotone in group size, the pipeline has a bug or an outlier-handling interaction that must be diagnosed before any arm is compared.

Mechanism. Weight-only quantization stores a low-bit integer per weight plus a shared scale (and optionally zero-point) per group. Smaller groups mean more scales, which better track local dynamic range and reduce error, at the cost of more metadata bytes and more dequantization work per output element. So group size trades the very quantity WOQ is meant to reduce, bytes read, against accuracy. Reporting a single "4-bit" number without stating group size is therefore under-specified: g=128 and g=32 are materially different artifacts with different memory footprints and different kernel efficiency. Separately, transformer activations and weights contain a small number of high-magnitude channels; a scheme that does not treat them specially will let those channels dominate the group's scale and crush the remaining weights into a few levels, which is the dominant quality failure mode and is invisible in a mean-error metric.

Boundary conditions. The monotonicity claim assumes a fixed scheme and fixed calibration set, varying only group size. It can break legitimately when the kernel changes at certain group sizes, or when an outlier-preserving mechanism is enabled only for some configurations. Those are confounds to be controlled, not exceptions to be waved through.

Controlled experiment. Sweep group size over a pre-registered ladder (per-tensor, 256, 128, 64, 32) with everything else fixed, plus a second factor: outlier handling on or off. For each cell record the effective bits per weight including scale and zero-point metadata, so the memory axis is honest. Evaluate on the frozen suite with slices, and separately compute per-channel weight reconstruction error to connect the quality outcome to a mechanism.

Measurements. Effective bits/weight (computed, MEASURED from artifact sizes); per-slice quality with CIs; per-channel max absolute reconstruction error and the count of channels above a threshold; decode TPOT per cell; HBM weight footprint per cell.

Confounders. Kernel availability differing by group size making the speed axis non-comparable; the calibration set interacting with outlier detection; evaluation noise exceeding the effect being resolved at fine group sizes; and comparing effective bits without counting metadata.

Numbers. Metadata overhead arithmetic, as an ESTIMATE from the format definition: at g=128 with fp16 scale and int4 zero-point, metadata adds roughly (16+4)/128 = 0.16 bits/weight; at g=32 it is roughly 0.63 bits/weight, so a nominal 4-bit scheme is really about 4.16 versus 4.63 effective bits. That difference is small in memory but the quality difference between those two cells is frequently the whole argument, which is why the sweep is mandatory rather than optional.

Evidence required and rollback. Pick the operating point from the measured quality-versus-effective-bits curve and publish the whole curve, not the chosen point. Roll back to the next-larger effective-bits cell, not to BF16, as the graduated response if a quality regression appears in production; keep BF16 as the terminal fallback reachable by one config flip.

corrected_answer:
Analytical stance under test: decision-cost-of-the-study-first - the experiment must be cheaper than the decision it informs, or the correct action is to skip it.

Hypothesis H50: the fully loaded cost of running this comparison to a defensible standard is less than 20 percent of the annual saving it could unlock; if not, the rational action is to either shrink the study to a screening design or forgo quantization entirely and revisit when the fleet is larger.

Mechanism. Every preceding stance adds arms, repeats, and suites, and each is individually justified. Summed, a rigorous WOQ evaluation is a multi-week program consuming GPU-hours for calibration, evaluation, and load testing, plus engineer time for harness work, safety review, and rollout. Meanwhile the benefit is bounded: it is at most the fraction of the inference bill attributable to the layers WOQ accelerates, times the realized speedup, times the fraction of that speedup that actually removes replicas. Capacity is quantized in whole replicas, so a 15 percent throughput gain on a 6-replica fleet may remove zero replicas and save nothing. The study cost is roughly fixed while the benefit scales with fleet size, so there is a fleet size below which the study is negative-value regardless of how well it is executed. Computing that threshold first is the discipline this stance imposes.

Boundary conditions. The calculus changes if the constraint is not money but a hard capacity ceiling (no more GPUs available at any price), or a memory ceiling that blocks a longer context window or a larger model. In those cases quantization is enabling rather than cost-saving and should be evaluated against the value of the blocked capability, not against a savings percentage. It also changes if the same evaluation harness will be reused for future model launches, in which case most of the engineer cost is an amortizable investment and should be allocated across those launches, not charged entirely to this decision.

Controlled experiment. Before any GPU is booked, run the arithmetic as a written pre-study: current monthly inference spend attributable to the target model (MEASURED from billing); decode share of GPU time (MEASURED from a one-week instrumentation window); a range of plausible realized speedups (ESTIMATE, stated as a low/central/high triple with reasoning); the replica-count granularity and the resulting step function from speedup to replicas removed (computed); and the study cost in GPU-hours and engineer-days (ESTIMATE from the harness plan). Then run a two-day screening experiment at the smallest defensible scale to see whether the central speedup estimate is even plausible, and only fund the full program if it survives.

Measurements. Monthly spend, decode GPU-time share, replicas at peak, replica granularity, screening-experiment TPOT delta with a CI, and the study's own accumulated GPU-hours tracked as it runs.

Confounders. Counting engineer time as free; ignoring the ongoing dual-path maintenance cost after rollout; assuming continuous rather than integer replica savings; and using list GPU prices when the fleet is on a committed-use discount.

Numbers. The 20 percent gate is an ESTIMATE and a policy choice, not a derived optimum; state it explicitly so a reviewer can argue for a different gate. Every currency figure must be labelled MEASURED (from billing) or ESTIMATE (from a model), with the model written down.

Evidence required and rollback. Require the pre-study arithmetic in the approval packet, and require it to be re-run with actual numbers after the screening phase. The rollback for this stance is organizational: if the screening result puts the central speedup below the replica-removal threshold, stop the program and record the negative result, which is a legitimate and reusable finding rather than a failure.
